subject_line: The yarmulke in the suit pocket in Yarmulkes & Fitted Caps
email_body:
Dear Aaron,

In Yarmulkes & Fitted Caps, the image of a yarmulke tucked into a suit pocket every Saturday, and of the star slipping to a back pocket in "Payos for Cornrows," stays with me as a precise picture of growing up Black and Jewish in Providence. I'd love to ask how those poems look to you now, more than a decade after Write Bloody published the book.

subject_line: The family farm behind Our Blue Earth
email_body:
Dear Richard,

Our Blue Earth stands out among your books for turning back to the family farm in Blue Earth, Minnesota, after collections as formally driven as Honey, with its hundred microsonnets. I'd be curious to hear how writing about the place you grew up differed from the compression those microsonnets demanded, and whether the farm had been waiting in the earlier books all along.

book_title: Shake Terribly the Earth: Stories from an Appalachian Family
subject_line: Writing family in Shake Terribly the Earth
email_body:
Dear Sarah Beth,

Shake Terribly the Earth draws its essays from a rural, Fundamentalist Christian childhood in Appalachia, and it's striking how much of a family's private history the book is willing to hold up to the light. I'd love to ask how you decided what belonged on the page, and whether teaching nonfiction in Stillwater has changed how you think about writing the people closest to you.

subject_line: The letter F that governs Fatal
email_body:
Dear Kimberly,

In Fatal, I was struck by how a constraint as strict as poems built around the letter F sits alongside material as raw as the book's reckoning with loss. It made me think of the Renaissance poets you teach at BYU, who so often trusted form to carry grief. I'd love to ask how that formal frame shaped what the poems were able to say.
